query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a controlled multi-step forging at 900–1000°C with a short-time annealing step to an as-cast eutectic HEA will refine the lamellar-colony microstructure and thereby concurrently increase room-temperature tensile strength and ductility compared to the unmodified baseline.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar-colony microstructure
generation.intervention: Multi-step forging at intermediate temperature (900–1000°C) under moderate strain rate, followed by a short-time annealing
generation.conditions: Forging temperature and strain rate must be adjusted to avoid excessive coarsening or damage; annealing must be brief to stabilize refined lamellae without overaging
generation.structural_mediator: Reduced lamellar spacing and strengthened internal colony boundaries
generation.mechanism: Progressive breaking and rearrangement of initial lamellae during forging promotes refined microstructure; short annealing keeps lamellae fine and cohesive, attenuating stress concentrations for enhanced ductility and blocking dislocation motion for improved strength
generation.predicted_outcome: Concurrently higher yield strength and improved room-temperature tensile elongation versus the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline
generation.baseline: Untreated eutectic HEA with characteristic dual-phase lamellar colonies that exhibit limited tensile ductility
generation.boundary: Benefit requires forging temperatures in the 900–1000°C range with suitable strain rates; overly high temperatures or prolonged annealing can coarsen lamellae and degrade strength or ductility
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative gain in strength–ductility synergy is not precisely known under the specified set points, but empirical data from related alloys support an improvement under proper conditions

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two batches of eutectic HEA: one in the as-cast lamellar-colony condition (control), the other subjected to multi-step forging at 900–1000°C under moderate strain rates and a short anneal. Evaluate resulting microstructures (lamellar spacing) via electron microscopy and perform tensile tests at room temperature.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the forged-and-annealed alloy exhibits no simultaneous improvement in yield strength and tensile elongation compared to the as-cast baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: In another study by Gwalani et al., FCC solid solution of Al0.3CoCrFeNi was tailored to produce triplex microstructure containing FCC, B2 and sigma via thermomechanical processing which resulted in a 400% increase in yield strength. Fu et al. studied the effect of Ti addition on Al0.6CoNiFe and they reported a high compressive yield stress of 2200 MPa and 6.2% ductility for spark plasma sintered Al0.6CoFeNi. The microstructure consisted of a mixture of ultra-fine FCC and BCC grains along with L12 precipitates in FCC phase. Addition of even higher amounts of Al in 3d transition element-based high entropy alloys (HEAs) can result in a eutectic FCC/B2 + BCC lamellar microstructure, which can also be rationalized based on the inability of a single FCC phase accommodating a high Al content. The room-temperature strength of Al0.3CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys (HEAs) is relatively low owing to its intrinsic fcc structure. In the present study, the as-cast HEAs were subjected to cold rolling and subsequent annealing treatment (800, 900, and 1000 °C) to adjust the microstructures and tensile properties. This treatment process resulted in the partial recrystallization, full recrystallization, and grain coarsening with increasing the annealing temperature. It was found that the large and spherical B2 precipitates were generated in the recrystallized grain boundaries of three annealing states, while the small and elongated B2 precipitates were aligned along the deformation twins in the non-recrystallized region of the 800 °C-annealing state. The former B2 precipitates assisted in refining the recrystallized grains to quasi ultra-fine grain and fine grain regimes (with the grain sizes of ~0.9, ~2.2, and ~7.2 μm). The tensile results indicated that the decreased annealing temperature induced the gradual strengthening of this alloy but also maintained the ductility at the high levels. chosen.technique: multi-step forging followed by short-time annealing
chosen.conditions: forging at 900–1000°C with moderate strain rates and final short annealing, followed by room-temperature tensile testing
chosen.why: We hypothesize that controlled multi-step forging and short-time annealing will refine the lamellar structure, reduce internal stress concentrations, and strengthen colony boundaries, thereby mitigating microcrack initiation and enabling enhanced ductility at room temperature without sacrificing strength. Prior studies of lamellar-refined microstructures in multi-principal element systems and steels support this approach. The predicted outcome is an increase in yield strength with a concurrent increase in tensile elongation compared to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, valid as long as forging temperature and strain rates are optimized to avoid excessive coarsening or damage. A direct tensile comparison of microstructure-treated samples versus untreated controls at room temperature would falsify the hypothesis if no concurrent improvement in strength and tensile ductility is observed.
